what_its_for: This medicine is used to treat multiple myeloma, a type of blood cancer that affects plasma cells in your bone marrow. It may also be used to treat light chain (AL) amyloidosis, a condition where abnormal proteins build up in your organs. It works by helping your immune system find and destroy cancer cells.
how_to_take: This medicine is given as a shot (injection) under the skin of your stomach (abdomen), not into a vein. A healthcare provider will give you this injection in a clinic or hospital setting. Each injection takes about 3 to 5 minutes. Before each injection, you will receive pre-medications (such as antihistamines, steroids, and fever-reducing medicines) to lower the chance of a reaction. Do NOT try to inject this medicine yourself at home unless your healthcare provider specifically trains and instructs you to do so.
dosing: Your doctor will decide your dose and how often you receive it based on your specific condition and treatment plan. Typically, doses are given more frequently at the start of treatment (such as weekly or every 2 weeks) and then spaced out to once every 4 weeks as treatment continues. Always follow your doctor's exact schedule. Never change your dose or schedule without talking to your doctor first.
missed_dose: If you miss or have to reschedule an appointment, contact your healthcare team right away. Do not try to make up a missed dose on your own. Your doctor will reschedule your next injection and may adjust your treatment calendar. It is very important to stay on your scheduled treatment plan as much as possible.
storage: This medicine is stored and handled by your healthcare provider or pharmacy. It must be kept refrigerated between 36°F and 46°F (2°C to 8°C). It should be kept in its original carton to protect it from light. It should NOT be frozen or shaken. If you are ever given this medicine to take home for any reason, keep it refrigerated and use it within the timeframe your pharmacist or doctor tells you.
what_to_avoid: Avoid live vaccines (such as the shingles vaccine Zostavax, nasal flu spray, or yellow fever vaccine) during treatment and for some time after, unless your doctor approves. Talk to your doctor before getting any vaccines. Let all of your healthcare providers know you are on this medicine, especially before any blood transfusions, because this drug can interfere with blood type testing and cross-matching. Avoid close contact with people who are sick, as this medicine can lower your ability to fight infections. Avoid activities that increase your risk of bleeding or bruising.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or go to the emergency room right away if you experience: trouble breathing, wheezing, or shortness of breath; chest tightness or pain; severe cough; throat tightness or swelling; dizziness or lightheadedness; fever, chills, or signs of infection; nausea, vomiting, or severe stomach pain; unusual bleeding or bruising; extreme tiredness or weakness; numbness or tingling in your hands or feet; swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat; or any new or worsening symptoms. Also notify your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding.
when_it_works: This medicine starts working right away at the cellular level, but you may not feel or notice the effects immediately. Your doctor will monitor your progress with regular blood tests and other evaluations. Some patients begin to see improvements in a few weeks to months. Every patient responds differently, so it is important to keep all of your appointments and stay in contact with your healthcare team.
special_populations: Pregnancy and Breastfeeding: This medicine may harm an unborn baby. Women who can become pregnant should use effective birth control during treatment and for 3 months after the last dose. Do not breastfeed during treatment and for 3 months after the last dose. Tell your doctor right away if you become pregnant. Elderly Patients: Older adults can receive this medicine, but may need to be monitored more closely for side effects. Kidney or Liver Problems: Tell your doctor if you have kidney or liver problems, as this may affect how the medicine works or is tolerated in your body.
